newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: University chief keeps job in blow to protesters.
newsitem.headline: University chief keeps job in blow to protesters.

text.p: In a bitter blow to the Serbian pro-democracy movement, the Socialist-dominated Belgrade University Council on Wednesday voted to keep rector Dragutin Velickovic in his post.
The decision was a snub to demands by students protesting for weeks against election fraud in Serbia and a promise by the Serbian government that he would be ousted.

The 76-member Belgrade University Council voted in secret ballot 41 against and 25 in favour of the no-confidence motion in the rector. Three ballots were invalid, two members did not vote and five were absent.
Half of the members of the Council are officials appointed by the ruling Socialist Party. The other half are deans, professors and students from various faculties.
Before the results of the vote were announced, Council deputy chairman Vlajko Brajic, a professor at the Belgrade Law Faculty, submitted his resignation because, he said, he was "told how to vote".
Some 2,000 students assembled in front of the rectoral offices erupted in fury when they heard the results.

"We are appalled, chilled, frozen by the decision. But let them, it's their democratic right," Cedomir Antic, a student leader, said. "We announce that our protest will last until the fulfilment of our demands and victory."
Velickovic remained unruffled. "I will be only too happy to continue my duties. The students are my soft spot," he said.
The students accuse Velickovic of persecution and obstruction of their demonstrations.
After the vote was announced, students lunged at Serbian Education Minister Dragoslav Mladenovic after he left the rectorate building, witnesses said.
Security guards barely managed to save the minister, who escaped unhurt into the nearby SPS headquarters.

The students had been demonstrating separately from the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition for the past 59 days against theft of opposition election victories in 14 of the biggest Serbian cities on November 17.
They demand reinstatement of Zajedno's victory and punishment of those involved in the election fraud, free access to media and sacking of the University rector.
Two Serbian deputy prime ministers last Saturday signed a statement saying all student demands would be met.
Student leaders accused the Council of duplicity.
"We are devastated and ashamed at the hypocrisy of the members of the Council who publicly voted in one way and secretly in another," one student leader said.
Before voting to keep the rector, the Council, in a public vote, endorsed the Serbian government statement, which had also been backed by the University Teaching Board on Monday.
"The University Council accepts stands of the Belgrade University Teaching Board in which full support is extended to demands of the student protest," it said.

The Council also called for a "full normalisation of classes as soon as all student demands are fulfilled and also accepts stands in the statement issued after the meeting of students and Serbian government deputy prime ministers".
The statement led the students to believe that the sacking of the rector was a foregone conclusion.
The controversy came in the middle of a bitter power struggle among moderates and hardliners within the ruling SPS and Yugoslav United Left and indicated diehards were gaining the upper hand.
